generator_view.scenario: A daily tea drinker makes four or five cups from inexpensive supermarket bags and is considering whether a roughly 30-dollar premium loose-leaf tin is worth it. Four exact frozen seller pages create a deliberately awkward comparison: Nina's is 34.00 dollars and its title says 2.8 ounces while the body says a 3.5-ounce or 100-gram loose-tea tin; T2 is a 16.50-dollar 100-gram loose-leaf box with multiple sizes and styles listed and no posted review aggregate; Hyleys is a 7.70-dollar 100-gram flavored loose-leaf tin rated 68 percent over twelve reviews; and Twinings is a 9.26-dollar 100-count English Breakfast bag offer rated 48 percent over twelve reviews. These offers differ in flavoring, blend, form, dose information, and seller wording, so their prices and ratings cannot isolate a loose-leaf effect. Concept evidence says cultivar, plucked-leaf quality, processing, blending, grading, particle size, CTC manufacture, dose, temperature, and steep time can all change the cup; it also says expensive fannings can be more flavorful than cheap whole leaf and that standardized sensory brewing is for meaningful comparison rather than an everyday recipe. Community pages supply only individual examples of a favorite tea, a kettle contaminant masquerading as a recipe change, inconsistent chai preparation, a desire to inspect infusers, and local loose-tea availability. The task is to separate a causal format question from a personal purchase question, normalize actual cost per accepted cup, and use a predeclared taste-per-dollar cutoff instead of assuming that loose leaf, a tin, a higher price, or a seller rating means better tea.
generator_view.target: Decide whether any of the exact loose-leaf offers is worth buying for this four-or-five-cup daily drinker without turning a tin, loose-leaf label, price, store aggregate, general processing or grading mechanism, or community anecdote into taste or value proof. Audit the exact offer and measurement fields; explain what processing, grading, CTC, black-tea brewing, and the four community pages can and cannot establish; separate a closest-feasible plain matched bag-versus-loose format trial from a separately labeled personal-preference trial of the actual unmatched drinks; measure dose, resteeps, accepted yield, waste, equipment, and delivered cost; and apply the predeclared seven-of-ten blind preference, one-point median score, no-recurring-defect, and 0.20-dollar incremental effective-cost-per-accepted-cup gates. End with the cheapest exact passing option, the bag baseline, or deferral, and do not name a universal format winner.
